articles.title: Back to the future
articles.content: THE collapse oftalksbetween the government and opposition and sharpening of their confrontation have again put the country on edge. PTI leaders announced they would go ahead with their protest march on Islamabad. Federal ministers vowed to stop this and renewed threats to impose governor’s rule and emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. PTI leaders, in turn, warned the government against taking such a step. It seems that a draft agreement was drawn up but the two sides could not close the gap on key issues. Both sides attributed the breakdown in negotiations to the other. These conflicting accounts make it hard to determine what were the precise sticking points that produced the deadlock. No further round of talks is planned. Instead, Islamabad has again become ‘containeristan’ with barricades erected across the city to prevent protesters from entering the capital. It is unclear whether the threat to impose governor’s rule was a pressure tactic and brinkmanship by the government or a serious option. Either way, it signals the government’s willingness to wield it as a sword of Damocles over the opposition. That, arguably, is the most concerning aspect of this latest confrontation. One after another, federal ministers warned that if conditions demanded, governor’s rule and emergency could be declared, without, however, specifying those conditions. For his part, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, a PPP leader, described governor’s rule as a “measure of necessity”, saying the president could take this action on the prime minister’s advice if the situation in the province so warranted. Some federal ministers tried to build a rationale for the move by accusing the KP government of governance failures and mishandling the rising wave of terrorism in the province. One senior minister accused the PTI government of “facilitating terrorists”. This was unfortunate as it showed the government was prepared to weaponise the terrorism issue to demonise its opponents. Statements by ministers after the talks broke down echoed these accusations against PTI. Our history shows that ousting provincial governments has always ended badly for the country. It was not the first time the present political dispensation in Islamabad threatened to impose governor’s rule. Such threats have surfaced in the past too, especially when PTI announced a march from KP to Islamabad. But this time, the threats were more sustained and sounded more serious. Significantly, they were repeated in the talks. These threats recall the country’s unedifying political experience in the past. Ousting provincial governments has a long pedigree in Pakistan’s turbulent political history. Every province of the country has been placed under governor’s rule at one time or another. Not long after the country’s independence, provincial governments began to be summarily dismissed by the central government in an early display of political intolerance and creeping authoritarianism. The first government to be toppled was in Punjab in 1949. That inglorious tradition persisted through the decades. In the 1970s, opposition-run provincial governments in KP and Balochistan were dismissed by prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. This had dire consequences for national unity. It weakened the federation and made a mockery of democracy. It deepened alienation among smaller provinces, fuelled regional sentiment, and led to the insurgency in Balochistan in the 1970s. While its roots could be traced back to the 1950s, it intensified during the 2000s and had lasting ramifications. The country is still struggling to deal with the deleteriousconsequences of repeatedly depriving the province of legitimately elected representative governments. History, however, is a poor teacher in Pakistan. Its lessons continue to be ignored. If the government is still contemplating imposing governor’s rule or emergency, it should understand that it will neither bring political calm to the province nor eliminate its political opponents. On the contrary, it will escalate the confrontation between the government and PTI-led opposition. The KP government enjoys two-thirds support in the provincial assembly. Ousting a government having a popular mandate would be fraught with many risks. It will be a blow to the federation, and to democracy. It will inevitably provoke a reaction, which even the use of force may not be able to control. Such an action will multiply the challenges for the federal authorities. They will have to confront and manage several fronts: PTI, the public, Pakhtun nationalists (leaders of the banned Pakhtun Tahaffuz Movement are already in jail) and militants/terrorists. Afghanistan can also be added to this as the hot and volatile border continues to pose serious security challenges for the country. The absence of a representative government will hardly make it easier to counter terrorism and militancy. On the contrary, that task will become tougher by the lack of public support as well as the political chaos that might ensue from such a move. The problems of installing and sustaining a non-representative set-up will also serve as a distraction from efforts to fight terrorism. If history is any guide ousting opposition-run provincial governments has always ended badly for those taking such action — but above all, for the country. It created political instability and deepened public disaffection in the concerned province. Other than secure temporary control of a province, it did not enable the federal government to achieve its aim of subduing its opponents and eroding their public support. There is speculation that once the protest march is over the hybrid government might move ahead with its plan of provincial re-engineering to redraw provincial boundaries and create new administrative units. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi recently repeated the call for a‘system reset’. This may involve legal manoeuvres to sidestep the constitutional requirement to secure the affected province’s prior consent to such changes. How consent of its political ally, the PPP, will be obtained is an open question as the party is vehemently opposed to Sindh’s division. Proceeding with provincial restructuring on which there is no national consensus will lack legitimacy and only divide the country. It will be even more disastrous if it is done on the back of removing the KP government. If history is not to repeat itself as tragedy, a modus vivendi has to be reached between the government and opposition. At the same time, the government should realise the serious repercussions of toppling a provincial government with a popular mandate. Going down this path will put the country’s future at stake. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: Humanising medicine
articles.content: “Medicine became distinguished when specialised knowledge was used for the benefit of the patient. It became noble when the needs of the patient held sway over the interests of the practitioner”— Rosenberg, 1987 IN Pakistan, discussions about healthcare usually revolve around the number of hospitals, doctors, hospital beds, ventilators, medicines, and health budget. This is important, but there is another crisis that is harder to measure and frequently ignored: the gradual loss of humanity from medicine. To humanise medicine is not merely to ask doctors to be kinder or improve their bedside manner. It is to recognise that healthcare is, at its core, a relationship between human beings. A sick person is not a diagnosis, a bed number, a laboratory report or a source of revenue. Nor is illness simply a technical problem to be fixed with increasingly sophisticated machines and medicines. People become ill within families, communities and societies. They bring to hospitals not only symptoms, but fear, poverty, uncertainty, grief and hope. Pakistan’s fragmented health system makes this human connection particularly difficult. At one end are government-run facilities, which are overwhelmed, understaffed and under-resourced. At another, there is the fee-for-service private sector, where access depends on one’s ability to pay. In between are charitable hospitals, which provide an invaluable service but cannot compensate for the failures of the national system. The result is that healthcare in Pakistan is a lottery in which the patient’s income determines not only where they receive treatment, but how quickly and with what degree of dignity. A hospital may possess the latest machines and still treat people without dignity. Private healthcare in Pakistan is particularly troubling. More than half of health expenditure is financed through out-of-pocket spending, and a large proportion of this goes to private facilities. The burden falls heavily on households already struggling with inflation. For a wealthy patient, illness may be frightening. For a poor patient, it can be financially catastrophic. Hence the question of humanising medicine becomes inseparable from the question of justice. There is little humanity in telling a patient that a potentially lifesaving treatment exists but is beyond their means or dignity in a family selling assets or borrowing to pay for treatment. Nor is there compassion in a healthcare system where a consultation may last only a few minutes because the clinician must see a large number of patients to generate revenue. The dehumanisation of medicine is not caused by individual doctors alone, who are themselves frequently victims of an inhuman system. A doctor in an overcrowded government hospital is expected to see scores of patients, or a nurse is responsible for far more patients than she can reasonably care for. It is easy to accuse healthcare professionals of becoming indifferent. It is harder to acknowledge that chronic exhaustion can turn empathy into a luxury. A humane healthcare system must therefore care for its carers. Medicine cannot be humanised by demanding compassion from doctors while denying them reasonable working conditions, professional security and psychological support. Burnout is not an individual weakness to be treated through resilience workshops. It is the consequence of a system that expects healthcare workers to compensate for institutional failure. A humanised medicine recognises the patient as a participant in decisions about their treatment. It involves explaining illness in language that patients and families can understand, acknowledging uncertainty rather than pretending that medicine has all the answers, and asking not only, ‘what disease does this person have?’ but also, ‘what has this illness done to this person’s life?’ Two people with the same diagnosis may have entirely different needs. A financially well-off person with diabetes may struggle with diet and exercise. Another may be choosing between purchasing insulin and feeding their family. Prescribing the same medication to both may not constitute the same quality of care. Humanising medicine requires clinicians to understand the social conditions in which illness occurs — poverty, unemployment, poor housing, gender inequality, violence and political instability — all enter the consultation room, whether doctors recognise them or not. In Pakistan, the weakness of the government healthcare system has pushed many patients towards the private sector that now dominates a substantial portion of healthcare delivery. Government services struggle with infrastructure, workforce, and quality challenges. A system dominated by fee-for-service incentives creates an uncomfortable question: what happens when the financial interests of an institution and the needs of a patient do not align? Charitable institutions demonstrate that Pakistanis possess a remarkable capacity for compassion and philanthropy. But charity cannot substitute for the state’s responsibility to ensure equitable access to healthcare. A citizen should not have to depend on the availability of a benefactor for treatment of a common illness. Healthcare is the state’s responsibility and cannot be based on the assumption that some will pay, some will donate, and the rest will wait. Ultimately, humanising medicine requires us to return to a simple principle: healthcare is not a commodity like any other. Markets can play a role, charitable organisations can make vital contributions, and private medicine will remain an important part of Pakistan’s healthcare landscape. But there is a need to invest in public healthcare (especially primary care), reduce the financial burden of medicines and tests, regulate private medicine, and build systems in which continuity, communication, and quality matter as much as procedures and profits. We need hospitals where patients are treated with dignity regardless of their class, doctors who have the time and institutional support to listen, and medical education that values communication and empathy alongside anatomy and pharmacology. Technological sophistication is not the same as humane care. A hospital may possess the latest machines and still treat people without dignity. At its most fundamental level, medicine begins when one vulnerable human being turns to another for help. Humanising medicine means ensuring that, regardless of wealth or status, the answer is not determined by how much the patient can pay. A civilised healthcare system is not only one with advanced medicine but also one that treats the person who cannot afford to be ill. The writer is professor emeritus of psychiatry at Aga Khan University.
articles.author: Murad Moosa Khan

articles.title: Teaching impact
articles.content: “WHAT do great teachers do?” I was asked this question recently. While there is no ‘right’ answer, there is an obvious and simplistic one. Great teachers don’t just teach; they connect with students in ways that make learning inspiring. Great teachers instil a hunger to know and do more. Great teachers help students enhance their skills. Great teachers create a love of learning and empower their students. On World Teachers’ Day today, it’s vital to revisit the role of teachers in the lives of their students. The impact of teaching doesn’t necessarily come from results — that is a small part of a teacher’s role. World Teachers’ Day reminds us that a teacher’s role encompasses much more than producing outcomes and enabling achievement. Their influence echoes through communities, workplaces, and nations. Interestingly, in Pakistan, one in four public primary schools are single-teacher schools. For thousands of students, their single teacher is not only responsible for delivering curriculum content but is also a nurturer, mentor, guide, and role model. A teacher has the power to create or break possibilities for students and to build or deflate self-esteem in children. Great teachers invest time and patience in their students’ potential. They don’t give up when faced with silence, procrastination, or defiance. They know how to steer their student towards self-belief and celebrate small steps forward. It is these exceptional qualities that students remember in a teacher long after they leave school. Students face hundreds of challenges in an increasingly complex and uncertain environment. Many have never seen family stability or received due care from a loved one. When students interact with teachers, they look for an adult who believes in their ability. More often, students work for a teacher than for a subject and do well to fulfil their teachers’ expectations. It’s vital to revisit the role of teachers in the lives of students. Steering expectations, commitment to building students’ confidence, and believing in their potential are qualities embedded in the personality and skills of a great teacher. World Teachers’ Day celebrates these ordinary daily miracles that nurture, protect, and help young minds bloom. Unlocking potential starts with developing intrinsic motivation, which is a student’s willingness and drive to learn without external incentives or pressure. Motivation is cultivated through a wide-ranging list of factors that contribute to holistic development. Well-being, social and emotional development in the early years, 21st-century competencies, progress markers such as learning portfolios, etc, are all part of a package that builds motivation. How independently and willingly students work is an indicator of the collective impact of this effort. Many successful education systems globally recognise the need to assess teaching and learning through these indicators across school levels, not just through test results. The success of teachers rests on how well they implement these key indicators and how they use their judgement to do so. The impact of teaching and learning is seen in how well students respond in class, how they manage work independently, how they regulate their schedules and cope with the demands on their time, and how communicative their teachers are. In Singapore, for example, emphasis is on the thinking process, character development, values, resilience, and social and emotional well-being. When these key markers are in place, academic achievement ensues. Academic achievement is usually the outcome of a structured process focused on evidence-informed efforts leading up to excellence. It tracks what the students know and can demonstrate, not what they have memorised. Positive learning environments are not created by chance. They are the product of a collaborative and connected teachers’ community. When teachers are aligned in common goals through shared portfolios, presentations, and discussions, what follows is alignment across the board. The collective success of the teaching community presents itself in student engagement, high attendance, motivation, and a drive to achieve results. The impact of successful teaching can also be seen in the development of transferable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, communication, problem-solving, and resilience. These competencies lead to long-term impact that prepares students for future education, employment, and life beyond school. Successful teachers create environments where students thrive, not just survive, and the greatest impact is seen through student achievement in a range of key areas, which are all important if we are to produce responsible and capable citizens. The writer is a teacher educator, author and a Fellow of the Higher Education Academy, UK. The views above are her own and do not reflect those of her employer.
articles.author: Neda Mulji

articles.title: A word’s worth
articles.content: WORDS wander with us; carried in the knapsacks of soldiers and wanderers, entwined in the chains of slaves or stowed on the ships and caravans of traders. Travel and time tend to transform, and often we find these words return home as strangers and yet strangely familiar. Take the orange which, juicy and vitamin-C packed as it is, has also travelled around the world; stemming from the Dravidian and Sanskrit ‘naranga’, it went west into Persia and Arabia as ‘naranj’, riding the trade routes into Italy as ‘arancia’ before crossing the channel from France into England and ending up as the ‘orange’ in the mid-1300s, denoting both the fruit and colour. This raises an interesting question: what did the English call the colour orange when they hadn’t yet seen the fruit? The answer is ‘ġeolurēad’, meaning yellow-red. Ever wonder why we call cinnamon ‘darcheeni’ in this part of the world? Take that word apart, and you have ‘dar’, meaning bark, and ‘cheeni’, meaning (you guessed it) Chinese. And this is because this was a bark that came from China! And why do we call sugar ‘cheeni’? Simply because, while the granulated and unrefined shakkar was always used in the subcontinent, when the sugar-making process travelled West to China, they refined it (pun intended) into the crystalline white sugar we know, which took the name ‘cheeni’ when it returned to the subcontinent. Speaking of China, have you ever wondered why some of the world calls tea tea (or a variant like ‘te’ or ‘thee’), and the rest call it ‘cha’ (‘chai’ in our case), or some variant thereof? That’s because in Mandarin and inland dialects, the Chinese character for this drink is pronounced ‘cha’, and it is from these regions that the Silk Route brought chai overland to Persia, India, and the Middle East. The name stuck. But in the coastal Fujian province, while the character remained the same, it was pronounced ‘te’, and since the tea leaves reached Europe largely through seaborne trade carried on by the Dutch East India Company, we get the French ‘thé’, the German ‘tee’, and the English ‘tea’. The quest to discover humanity’s ‘natural’ language has led to abuses. Here’s one you may not have heard of: I’m hoping most of you have been to a desi barber for champi — the traditional head massage with oil – and, of course, I’m also hoping most of you have used shampoo at some point. But did you know that the words are related? Around 1814, a Bengali entrepreneur, Deen Muhammad, took the age-old champi to England, where he rechristened the process ‘shampooing’, while opening England’s first-ever shampoo parlour, setting himself up as a ‘Shampooing Surgeon’ in true Victorian style. And if you’re a fan of kebabs, it may delight you to know that you are the proud inheritor of a truly ancient culinary legacy, because the root of this word is the Akkadian ‘kababu’, which means to ‘roast over a fire’. Given that the Akkadian Empire ruled over 4,000 years ago, know that when you stare longingly at your latest bun kabab, millennia stare back at you approvingly. Now, while we know that Sumerian is the oldest identified written language, we have no idea what the first human languages sounded like, but it’s theorised that they would sound similar to the language of the San Bushmen of southern Africa with its clicking sounds or — if you subscribe to the ‘bow-wow theory’ — were inspired by animal calls and the sounds of nature. But the quest to discover humanity’s ‘natural’ language has led to terrible abuses throughout history in the form of language deprivation experiments. The theory was that if babies were deprived of language, they would spontaneously begin speaking a ‘natural’ or ‘divine’ language, which would thus reveal humanity’s first language. The idea is fascinating; the execution was incredibly cruel: Pharaoh Psamtik I is said to have handed over newborns to a shepherd with instructions never to speak to them, and while Herodotus claims the babies started speaking Phrygian, it’s unlikely the experiment was conducted with true scientific rigour. Motivated by his personal religious theory that the first language of man was Hebrew, the 15th-century King James of Scotland also supposedly isolated newborns on an island with a deaf-mute nurse to see if his theory held water. Mughal Emperor Akbar did the same, though the motivations were reportedly twofold: one, to see if the children would begin to speak a ‘divine’ language or the native language of their parents, and two, to see if the ability to speak was innate and not dependent on hearing. Akbar isolated newborns in a custom-built ‘gang mehal’ (‘house of the mute’) with caretakers who lacked the ability to speak. Unsurprisingly, by the time the unfortunate children were four years old, they could only vocalise grunts and basic guttural sounds. History does not record what became of them.
articles.author: Zarrar Khuhro

articles.title: After the talks
articles.content: THE nation was made to wait for all of Saturday as opposition and government representatives convened for thesecond timein as many days at Parliament House in Islamabad. Sadly, the wait did not pay off. Early on Sunday, opposition representatives said they had reached a deadlock and an understanding could not be reached with the government. Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas said talks broke down over allowing former prime minister Imran Khan to meet his personal physicians, as well as the question of how terrorism in KP is to be addressed. On Sunday afternoon, the interior minister accused KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi of‘sabotaging’the talks. It seems that there had been some understanding with the KP government that a signed agreement and implementation plan for counterterrorism operations would be finalised within 72 hours. But, this proposal was abandoned by Peshawar in the final phase over undisclosed reasons. It appears — though time will make it clearer — that Mr Afridi had insisted that his province and its legislature have the final say on any security decisions affecting KP’s people. Otherwise, the list of demands shared by him on social media — as his proposals to the committee — seemed rather straightforward. It seemed he was open to further political engagement while relief for Mr Khan and other incarcerated PTI leaders was sought through legal means rather than any extraordinary or extrajudicial steps. The draft also signalled that the KP government was open to working with the centre on counterterrorism, calling for “effective, consistent and meaningful” consultations between the two. It is, therefore, not clear why a middle ground could not be reached or what became a sticking point. Both sides will spin it to blame the other. The PTI has sincekicked offits protest march, as it had promised it would. Former KP chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur had set out with a caravan from D.I. Khan for Lakki Marwat as these words were being written. He was to be joined by the incumbent chief minister. The party seems to be taking great care to advertise it as a “peaceful political march”, while repeatedly urging protesters to refrain from violence or vandalism. Mr Afridi had earlier reiterated the constitutional right to protest peacefully; it appears that the messaging is intended to keep violent reprisals by the government at bay. In any case, the march is still far away from the federal capital. The question of where it ends up, though, will cause stress to the federal government. Perhaps the talks should not be abandoned completely, considering how close they came to a solution. The negotiators should reconvene to give the process another chance. The window has not closed and, in keeping with democratic tradition, both sides must do their utmost to keep it open.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Child safety online
articles.content: PAKISTANI children are spending more of their lives online, but the safeguards around them are not keeping pace. A recent Kasperskysurveycovering the Middle East, Turkiye, and Africa region, including Pakistan, found YouTube to be the most popular mobile app among children surveyed here, followed by Instagram and WhatsApp. The more important issue, however, is what children may face once they are online. Multiplayer games and communication platforms can put young users in direct contact with strangers. This can expose them to grooming, fraud, blackmail, and other forms of abuse. Generative AI has made the problem more complicated. Photos and videos shared online can now be altered into convincing fake images or clips and used for cyberbullying or harassment. The survey figures should not be treated as a complete picture of all Pakistani children, but the risks it highlights are serious. The problem is that while these dangers are growing, the state’s ability to respond remains unclear. The PTA hastold the Islamabad High Courtthat it does not have the legal authority to impose mandatory age checks or stop children under 16 from using social media. This should lead to a wider debate about how Pakistan protects children online. The answer cannot simply be to demand restrictions that a regulator may not have the power or technical means to enforce. The PTA has also noted that because major platforms use HTTPS encryption, regulators may be unable to block one harmful page or post without affecting access to the entire platform. At the same time, the2025 amendments to Pecaprovide for a new ‘Social Media Protection and Regulatory Authority’, raising questions about which body will ultimately be responsible and what powers it will have. Whatever system is put in place, it must go beyond blocking websites and apps. Social media platforms should be required to make children’s accounts safer, offer simple reporting tools, and respond quickly to grooming, fake content, and abuse. Any age-checking system must also protect privacy. Schools should teach children how to recognise online risks, while parents need to talk openly with them about strangers, personal information, and troubling online conversations. No single ban, parental control setting, or awareness campaign will be enough. Protecting children online will require clear laws, responsible technology companies, better digital education, and informed parents working together.
articles.author: Editorial
